This course covers the use of tools from data science (statistics, machine learning, and programming) to model climate hazards such as floods and droughts.
Through hands-on programming assignments based on state-of-the-art published research, students will learn to apply methods to real-world problems with a strong emphasis on probabilistic methods and uncertainty quantification.

### Learning Objectives

After completing this course, you will be able to:

**Module 1 - Extreme Value Analysis:** Apply extreme value theory from basic distribution fitting through hierarchical Bayesian models for regional precipitation analysis

**Module 2 - Semi-Empirical Models:** Build and validate semi-empirical physical models, implementing multiple uncertainty quantification approaches including bootstrap and MCMC

**Module 3 - Climate Model Integration:** Integrate observations with climate model output through bias correction and statistical downscaling methods

**Synthesis:** Strategically combine limited observational data with abundant but biased model simulations to characterize hydroclimate extremes under uncertainty

### Prerequisites & Preparation

* Linear algebra (you should be comfortable with matrix notation and basic operations)
* A course in applied statistics (e.g., STAT 419/519)
* Some exposure to Python, Julia, Matlab, R, or another programming language is strongly encouraged, though not strictly required

I will post a "Homework Zero" assignment before the start of the semester to help you assess your readiness for the course.

### Required Materials

No textbook is required for this course.
Reading will come from a [free, online textbook](https://dossgollin-lab.github.io/climate-risk-management-reference/) developed specifically for this class, or will be provided through Canvas.

You do need a computer that you are able to install software on to complete the assignments and participate in class activities.
If you do not have access to one, please contact me as soon as possible so that we can make arrangements.

### AI/LLM Resource Policy {#sec-llm}

The rapid evolution of AI tools raises important questions about learning, assessment, and the skills you need for the future.
AI tools, especially Large Language Models (LLMs), can be powerful aids in learning.
They can outline, summarize, explain, and write code.
However, these tools also pose risks, including the potential for plagiarism and for students to rely on them without developing their own understanding.

**The use of these models must be informed by our values and goals, and we must be critical in thinking about when and how to use them.**
For example, you may want to quickly get a plausible answer on a task, ensure you have the best possible answer on a task, develop your understanding of a particular topic, strengthen your long-term cognitive development, rapidly prototype an idea, or get feedback on something you have written.
Each of these goals may take you in a different direction with respect to your use of LLMs.
Depending on the task at hand, you may also wish to consider your relationship with the companies creating AI models, the potential risks and consequences of the topic you are working on, or the ethical implications of using these tools.
My goal is not to give you a single "right" answer, but to require you to think critically about your use of these tools and to **make deliberate choices**.

For this course, the goal of learning is articulated in the course learning objectives.
Rather than focusing on preventing or punishing "cheating," we recognize that students will use LLMs on take-home and written material, and should learn to do so responsibly.
Assessment will focus on approaches—including tests and in-class activities—that are not readily amenable to LLM use (note: the use of any hypothetical wearable AI device is prohibited).
You are encouraged to explore the resources linked on the [LLM resources page](resources/llm.qmd) and elsewhere.
This AI policy is **reciprocal**.
For example, your instructors may use LLMs to draft rubrics or add comments to example code, but your assignments will not be graded by LLMs, and we will not use LLMs to write code or text we do not understand and fully stand behind.

## Grading

Your final grade will be determined from a portfolio of work that includes regular low-stakes practice, in-class assessments of core concepts, and a final project.
The goal is to reward consistent engagement, practice, and deep, applied learning.

- **Weekly Quizzes (20%)** will assess your understanding of the course material. They will not test for deep understanding, but will give you immediate feedback if you start to fall behind. Your lowest quiz score will be dropped.
- **Problem Sets (10%)** on each module will reinforce your understanding of the material and provide practice with the skills you are learning. Problem sets are graded for completion to reward consistent effort and practice.
- **Labs (10%)** provide hands-on experience applying concepts and building technical skills. Labs are graded for completion to encourage exploration and learning from mistakes.
- **Module Tests (40%)** on each module will closely follow the problem sets to assess your understanding of the material and your ability to apply the skills you have learned. If you do and understand the problem set, you should do well on the test.
- **Final Project (20%)** is a semester-long, multi-stage assignment where you will perform a deep dive into a hydroclimate risk problem of your choosing. You will propose a research question and dataset, apply an advanced method to analyze it, and communicate your findings. Students are required to attend a one-on-one project check-in during office hours after their proposal is submitted. The final deliverables include: (1) a project proposal, (2) a final report written in the style of a new section for a textbook on a method you learned, and (3) a presentation to the class during our Course Symposium, effectively teaching your peers about the method and its application.

### Late Work Policy

Late work is not accepted.

If you need to miss a class because of major illness, family emergency, or other unavoidable conflict, or for critical research travel, please let me know as soon as possible.
In these cases, you will be assigned a score of 0/0, meaning it will not be reflected in the numerator or denominator.

### Remote Learning Policy

This course is designed for in-person attendance on Mondays and Wednesdays, and remote attendance on Fridays.
While a standing Zoom link has been created for the class, I will not livestream or record lectures unless specifically requested.
If you need to attend remotely, please ask in advance.
